findings.title: Access tokens issued together with an offline refresh token get the wrong ("online") session-type prefix in their ID
findings.body: initToken() encodes the token ID, including the session-type prefix, from the user session that exists at token-creation time. For an authorization-code or direct-grant request with scope=offline_access that session is the ONLINE session, so the ID gets the "on" prefix. However, afterwards TokenManager.AccessTokenResponseBuilder.generateRefreshToken() creates the offline user session and re-points accessToken.sessionState to the offline session (OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse even removes the online session for first-time offline access, which only works because the access token has been re-bound to the offline session). The result is that an access token bound to an OFFLINE session carries the "on" (online) prefix until the next refresh (refresh-minted tokens correctly get "of"). This corrupts exactly the data this PR exists to provide: a consumer relying on the session-type prefix to pick the right session lookup (follow-up #37662) would search online sessions, miss the offline session, and either reject a valid token or need the old fallback lookup anyway. The session type must be determined after the offline-session switch, or the token ID re-encoded when generateRefreshToken() rebinds the token to the offline session.

findings.title: New isAccessTokenId matcher never actually verifies the grant-type shortcut (inverted condition and wrong character offsets)
findings.body: The matcher added in this PR contains two mistakes in one line: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. First, the condition is inverted: it returns false (no match) when the extracted shortcut EQUALS the expected one, instead of when it does not. Second, the offsets are wrong: in the 6-character prefix (2 chars session type, 2 chars token type, 2 chars grant type) the grant shortcut occupies indexes 4-5, so it should be substring(4, 6); substring(3, 5) takes the second token-type character and the first grant-type character. Net effect: for real token IDs the extracted two characters essentially never equal the expected shortcut, so the matcher degrades to only checking that the part after ':' is a UUID, and expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken pass regardless of whether the encoded grant type is correct. If someone later fixes only the offsets, every one of those assertions will start failing because of the inverted equals. The whole purpose of these updated event assertions — verifying the new encoded context — is therefore not tested at all.

findings.title: New abstract getShortcut() method breaks existing custom OAuth2 grant providers with AbstractMethodError at server startup
findings.body: Adding a non-default method to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface is a hard breaking change for any deployment with a custom grant type: DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates ALL registered OAuth2GrantType factories and calls getShortcut() on each of them during server startup, so a custom factory compiled against the previous version of the interface will throw AbstractMethodError and prevent the server from booting. This should be a default method (e.g. deriving a shortcut from the factory id, or returning null that the encoder factory tolerates). Note also that a custom implementation returning null would currently kill startup as well, because ConcurrentHashMap.put() throws NullPointerException for the null shortcut in postInit().

findings.title: Constructor validates grantType twice and never checks rawTokenId for null
findings.body: The constructor has `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null grantType not allowed")` immediately followed by `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` — the second check was clearly meant to validate rawTokenId but re-checks grantType. As a result, an AccessTokenContext with a null rawTokenId is accepted despite the error message claiming otherwise, and DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId() will then silently concatenate null into the token ID, producing something like "onrtac:null" instead of failing fast. Change the second requireNonNull to check rawTokenId.

findings.title: Context.setFormParams() leaves the cached grantType field stale
findings.body: The Context constructor now derives the grantType field from formParams (`formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`), but the existing public setter setFormParams() replaces the formParams map without recomputing grantType. Any caller that swaps the form parameters after construction will have getGrantType() return the value from the original params, and that stale value is exactly what OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse() stores into the ClientSessionContext under Constants.GRANT_TYPE and what ends up encoded into the access-token ID. Either recompute grantType in setFormParams() or drop the cached field and read it from formParams in getGrantType().

findings.title: testIncorrectGrantType passes because of a NullPointerException, not the intended validation error
findings.body: The test builds the factory by hand and never calls postInit(), so the factory's sessionFactory field is null. When decoding "ofrtac:5678", getGrantTypeByShortcut("ac") does not find "ac" in the hand-built map and falls through to sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...), which throws a NullPointerException. The test catches the broad RuntimeException, so it goes green for the wrong reason and never exercises the intended path (unknown grant shortcut -> IllegalArgumentException "Unknown value 'ac' for grant type"). Catch IllegalArgumentException specifically and provide a stub/empty KeycloakSessionFactory so the real validation logic is tested.

findings.title: getShortcut() javadoc suggests 3-letter shortcuts, but the codec requires exactly 2 characters
findings.body: The javadoc says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters", yet every built-in implementation returns 2 characters and DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId() hard-codes a 6-character context prefix (2 chars each for session type, token type, grant type) and rejects anything else with "Expected length of 6". A grant implementation that follows the javadoc and returns a 3-character shortcut would produce token IDs that cannot be decoded later, and nothing in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() validates the shortcut length (it only checks uniqueness). The contract should state that shortcuts must be exactly 2 characters and postInit should enforce it, or the codec should be made length-agnostic.
